fig12_1_neuron_pathway.caption: Figure 12.1. Arrangement of first-, second-, and third-order neurons of the somatosensory system.

pins.label: Receptors
pins.note: Free nerve endings or specialized receptors transduce a stimulus (touch, temp, pain) into an electrical signal — the first step in somatosensation.

pins.label: First-order neuron
pins.note: Carries the signal from the receptor into the spinal cord; cell body sits in the dorsal root ganglion.

pins.label: Spinal cord
pins.note: First-order neuron synapses here (or travels up ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns before synapsing in the medulla, depending on the pathway).

pins.label: Second-order neuron
pins.note: Crosses (decussates) to the opposite side and ascends to the thalamus — this is why a spinal cord lesion on one side can cause sensory loss on the other side below the lesion.

pins.label: Thalamus (shown in purple)
pins.note: The sensory relay station of the brain. Thalamic stroke/damage can cause thalamic pain syndrome — severe, poorly controlled pain on the opposite body side.

pins.label: Third-order neuron
pins.note: Carries the signal from thalamus to cortex — the final relay before conscious perception.

pins.label: Primary somatosensory cortex
pins.note: Postcentral gyrus. This is where the stimulus becomes a conscious, localized sensation — damage here causes loss of fine touch discrimination without losing pain sensation.

pins.label: Tissue injury
pins.note: The triggering event — cell damage releases intracellular contents and triggers the inflammatory cascade.

pins.label: Inflammation
pins.note: Inflammatory cells and chemicals accumulate at the injury site, sensitizing nociceptors (peripheral sensitization).

pins.label: Mediator release
pins.note: Substance P, prostaglandins, serotonin, and acetylcholine directly stimulate or sensitize nociceptors. NSAIDs work by blocking prostaglandin synthesis here.

pins.label: Receptors (nociceptors)
pins.note: Free nerve endings that specifically respond to noxious (tissue-damaging) stimuli.

pins.label: Spinothalamic pathway
pins.note: The ascending pain pathway — crosses in the spinal cord then ascends contralaterally to the thalamus.

pins.label: RAS (reticular activating system)
pins.note: Pain signals passing through here trigger arousal/alertness — why pain keeps you awake and focused on the threat.

pins.label: Thalamus
pins.note: Relays the pain signal onward and contributes to the emotional/autonomic response to pain.

pins.label: Primary somatosensory cortex
pins.note: Where pain becomes consciously localized ('my hand hurts') rather than just a diffuse unpleasant feeling.

pins.label: Pain (conscious perception)
pins.note: The endpoint — note that everything before this is nociception (signal transmission); 'pain' itself is the subjective, conscious experience.

pins.label: Cornea
pins.note: Avascular, transparent — does most of the eye's light bending (refraction). Corneal abrasion is intensely painful because it's densely innervated.

pins.label: Anterior chamber
pins.note: Between cornea and iris, filled with aqueous humor. Where intraocular pressure is measured (tonometry).

pins.label: Iris
pins.note: The colored muscular diaphragm; controls pupil size via sphincter (parasympathetic/miosis) and dilator (sympathetic/mydriasis) muscles.

pins.label: Pupil
pins.note: The opening in the iris — not a structure itself, just the hole light passes through.

pins.label: Posterior chamber
pins.note: Between iris and lens, where aqueous humor is actually produced by the ciliary body before flowing into the anterior chamber.

pins.label: Lens
pins.note: Changes shape (via ciliary muscle) to focus light on the retina — accommodation. Loses elasticity with age (presbyopia) or clouds (cataract).

pins.label: Ciliary muscle
pins.note: Contracts to round the lens for near vision (accommodation) and produces aqueous humor. Also the site aqueous drains near in open-angle glaucoma.

pins.label: Vitreous humor
pins.note: Gel that fills the posterior cavity and maintains the eyeball's shape; does NOT recirculate like aqueous humor does.

pins.label: Retina
pins.note: Contains rods (dim light, peripheral) and cones (color, central). Detached retina = painless vision loss, an emergency.

pins.label: Fovea
pins.note: Center of the macula, cone-only, sharpest central vision — this is what's lost first in macular degeneration.

pins.label: Optic disk
pins.note: Where the optic nerve exits — has NO photoreceptors, so it's the physiologic 'blind spot.' Also where you look for papilledema/cupping (glaucoma).

pins.label: Optic nerve
pins.note: Cranial nerve II — carries the visual signal to the brain. Glaucoma causes progressive, irreversible optic nerve damage from sustained pressure.

pins.label: Superior rectus
pins.note: CN III (oculomotor) — elevates the eye.

pins.label: Superior oblique
pins.note: CN IV (trochlear) — the only muscle that passes through a pulley (trochlea); depresses and intorts the eye when it's turned inward.

pins.label: Medial rectus
pins.note: CN III — adducts the eye (turns it toward the nose). Weakness here causes an exotropia (eye drifts outward).

pins.label: Lateral rectus
pins.note: CN VI (abducens) — abducts the eye (turns it toward the ear). CN VI palsy causes an esotropia (eye drifts inward) and double vision.

pins.label: Inferior rectus
pins.note: CN III — depresses the eye.

pins.label: Inferior oblique
pins.note: CN III — elevates and extorts the eye when turned inward; the only extraocular muscle that originates from the front of the orbit, not the back.

fig12_11_ear_structures.caption: Figure 12.11. Structures of the external, middle, and internal ear.

pins.label: Auricle (pinna)
pins.note: Collects and funnels sound waves into the canal — purely external, cartilage-supported.

pins.label: External acoustic meatus
pins.note: The ear canal; cerumen (wax) here can impact and cause conductive hearing loss.

pins.label: Tympanic membrane (eardrum)
pins.note: Vibrates in response to sound pressure waves; what you see (bulging, red, perforated) on otoscopic exam.

pins.label: Malleus
pins.note: First and largest ossicle, attached directly to the eardrum.

pins.label: Incus
pins.note: Middle ossicle, bridges malleus and stapes.

pins.label: Stapes
pins.note: Smallest bone in the body; its footplate sits in the oval window and transmits vibration into the fluid-filled inner ear.

pins.label: Semicircular canals
pins.note: Detect rotational head movement — part of the vestibular (balance) system, not hearing.

pins.label: Cochlea
pins.note: Snail-shaped, fluid-filled; contains the organ of Corti where hair cells convert sound vibration into neural signal.

pins.label: Vestibule
pins.note: Contains the utricle and saccule — sense linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity.

pins.label: Auditory (eustachian) tube
pins.note: Connects middle ear to the nasopharynx; equalizes pressure. Dysfunction (common with colds, in children) causes otitis media with effusion.

fig13_2_hpa_axis.caption: Figure 13.2. The hypothalamic–pituitary axis regulates the release of hormones.

pins.label: Hypothalamus
pins.note: The master coordinator — integrates neural input (stimuli, neurotransmitters) and translates it into releasing/inhibiting hormones.

pins.label: Releasing hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH)
pins.note: Travel a tiny distance via the hypophyseal portal system directly to the anterior pituitary — not general circulation, so very small amounts have big effects.

pins.label: Posterior pituitary
pins.note: Not a true endocrine gland — it just STORES and releases ADH and oxytocin that were made in the hypothalamus and travel down the nerve axons.

pins.label: ADH and oxytocin
pins.note: Made in hypothalamic neurons, transported down axons, stored in the posterior pituitary until release.

pins.label: Anterior pituitary
pins.note: True endocrine tissue — synthesizes and secretes its own tropic hormones in response to hypothalamic releasing hormones.

pins.label: TSH → Thyroid gland
pins.note: Stimulates the thyroid to release T3/T4, which then negatively feedback on both the pituitary and hypothalamus.

pins.label: ACTH → Adrenal gland
pins.note: Stimulates cortisol release from the adrenal cortex — the core of the stress response axis.

pins.label: FSH/LH → Ovary/Testes
pins.note: Drives estrogen/testosterone production and the reproductive cycle.

pins.label: Prolactin → Breast
pins.note: Stimulates milk production; unlike other anterior pituitary hormones it's under tonic DOPAMINE INHIBITION rather than a releasing hormone — a dopamine-blocking drug can cause galactorrhea.

pins.label: Growth hormone → Bone and soft tissue
pins.note: Promotes growth via IGF-1 from the liver; excess in adults causes acromegaly, excess in children causes gigantism.

fig13_8_stress_response.caption: Figure 13.8. Stimulation of cortisol and catecholamines in the stress response.

pins.label: Hypothalamus
pins.note: Senses the stressor and starts the cascade by releasing CRH.

pins.label: CRH
pins.note: Corticotropin-releasing hormone travels to the anterior pituitary.

pins.label: Pituitary → ACTH
pins.note: Anterior pituitary releases ACTH into systemic circulation.

pins.label: Adrenal medulla → Catecholamines
pins.note: The brainstem/sympathetic pathway directly stimulates the adrenal medulla to dump epinephrine/norepinephrine — this is the FAST, seconds-scale fight-or-flight response, parallel to the slower hormonal cortisol pathway.

pins.label: Adrenal cortex → Cortisol
pins.note: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol — the SLOW, minutes-to-hours stress hormone that mobilizes glucose and suppresses inflammation/immunity.

pins.label: Autonomic nervous system manifestations
pins.note: Tachycardia, diaphoresis, pupil dilation — the visible signs of the fast catecholamine pathway, distinct from cortisol's metabolic effects.

fig13_10_diabetes_insipidus.caption: Figure 13.10. The mechanism of diabetes insipidus.

pins.label: Anterior / Posterior pituitary
pins.note: Central DI = the posterior pituitary (or hypothalamus) fails to make/release ADH. Nephrogenic DI = ADH is present but the kidney doesn't respond to it — same downstream picture, different cause.

pins.label: ADH deficiency
pins.note: Without ADH, the collecting duct's aquaporin water channels aren't inserted, so water can't be reabsorbed back into the blood.

pins.label: Collecting duct
pins.note: Normally the site where ADH makes the duct permeable to water, concentrating urine. In DI it stays impermeable.

pins.label: Impaired water reabsorption
pins.note: Water that should be pulled back into the bloodstream instead stays in the tubule and is lost as urine.

pins.label: Decreased renal water reabsorption
pins.note: The net kidney-level consequence — massive water loss in the urine.

pins.label: Inappropriately dilute urine
pins.note: The key diagnostic clue: urine that is dilute (low specific gravity) despite the patient being dehydrated/hypernatremic — urine should be concentrated in true dehydration, so dilute urine here is 'inappropriate.'

pins.label: Diabetes insipidus: polyuria, polydipsia
pins.note: Massive dilute urine output (polyuria) drives compensatory extreme thirst (polydipsia). Contrast with diabetes MELLITUS, where polyuria is from glucose osmotic diuresis, not ADH failure.
